blocks.text: 1. Types of Deep Learning Problems

blocks.alt: Deep learning problems split into image-based, sequence-based, and generative

blocks.text: The Deep Learning Workflow, the previous topic, previewed designing the network architecture as a genuinely new stage compared to the traditional Machine Learning workflow. Different Deep Learning problems genuinely need different architecture families, since a technique well-suited to images is often poorly suited to sequences of text, and vice versa.

This topic previews the major problem categories Deep Learning addresses, closing out this introductory module. Neural Network Fundamentals, the very next module, builds the shared mechanics every one of these categories actually relies on underneath its own specific architecture choices.
2. Image-Based Problems

blocks.alt: An image passes through a CNN into a class or bounding box

blocks.text: Image-based problems, covered throughout the CNN modules later in this course, span several genuinely distinct levels of difficulty. Image classification assigns one single label to an entire image, directly echoing the Computer Vision applications already covered in their own topic.

Object detection is a genuinely harder version, identifying and labeling multiple distinct objects and their locations within one single image, and image segmentation goes further still, labeling every single individual pixel in an image, the most granular, most demanding version of this entire problem family.

blocks.text: 3. Sequence Problems

blocks.alt: A sequence passes through an RNN or transformer into a next value or label

blocks.text: Sequence problems are ones where order genuinely matters to the actual meaning of the data. Time series forecasting predicts a future value directly from a sequence of past values in order, covered through the Sequence Models and Recurrent Neural Network modules later in this course.

Text is fundamentally a sequence too, a sentence is a specific, ordered sequence of words, and rearranging that order can change, or destroy, its meaning entirely. This is covered through several NLP-focused modules ahead, Recurrent Neural Networks, LSTM and GRU, and eventually Transformers, each building on the ones before it.
4. Generative Problems

blocks.alt: Noise or a prompt passes through a generative model into a new sample

blocks.text: Generative problems connect directly back to the Creative and Generative Applications already covered in the previous topic. These involve producing entirely new content, rather than labeling or classifying content that already exists.

Image generation, text generation, and considerably more fall into this category, all covered in genuine depth in the Generative Models module later in this course, exploring exactly how a network learns to produce new, original content rather than simply recognizing existing patterns.
5. Reinforcement-Style Problems

blocks.alt: An agent interacts with an environment to receive a reward

blocks.text: This connects back to Reinforcement Learning, already covered in genuine depth in the traditional Machine Learning course. Some Deep Learning systems combine deep networks directly with Reinforcement Learning's trial-and-error framework, using a network to represent the agent's learned knowledge instead of a simpler, traditional model.

This combined approach is called Deep Reinforcement Learning, briefly touched on in the Advanced Topics module later in this course, a genuinely distinct problem category from the image, sequence, and generative problems already covered earlier in this topic.
6. Matching Architecture to Problem

blocks.alt: A problem type leads to choosing the right architecture

blocks.text: The genuinely core skill this topic sets up for the rest of this course is recognizing what kind of problem is actually being solved, image-based, sequence-based, generative, reinforcement-style, or something else entirely, before choosing any specific technique.

Once that category is genuinely clear, choosing the architecture family already built to handle that specific kind of problem well becomes considerably more straightforward, exactly the reasoning this course's later modules, CNNs for images, Transformers for sequences, and so on, are organized around.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Getting comfortable identifying which problem category a new situation actually falls into is a genuinely practical skill worth returning to throughout the rest of this course, since it directly guides which later module actually applies.

blocks.text: 7. A Shared Foundation Underneath Every Category

Every one of these problem categories, image-based, sequence-based, generative, and reinforcement-style, still relies on the exact same core mechanics underneath its own specific architecture choices: neurons, layers, activation functions, loss functions, and backpropagation.

This is exactly why Neural Network Fundamentals, the very next module in this course, comes before any specific architecture family gets introduced, building that shared foundation first, so every later, more specialized module can build directly on top of concepts already covered rather than re-explaining them from scratch each time.
8. Real Problems Often Blend Categories

blocks.alt: Image captioning blends a vision part and a language part

blocks.text: Real Deep Learning problems often blend more than one of these categories together in practice. Image captioning, for instance, takes an image as input and produces a text sequence as output, directly combining image-based and sequence-based techniques within a single system.

Multimodal Deep Learning, its own dedicated module later in this course, covers systems that combine multiple data types together even more broadly, images and text together for instance, reflecting how real, deployed systems frequently do not fit neatly into just one single problem category.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Do not treat these categories as rigid, mutually exclusive boxes. Many of the most interesting, practically useful Deep Learning systems genuinely combine techniques from more than one category at once.

blocks.text: 9. Closing This Introductory Module

This closes the Introduction to Deep Learning module entirely, covering what Deep Learning actually is, why it genuinely works, its history from the Perceptron through modern Large Language Models, its real applications, its overall workflow, and now the major problem categories it addresses.

The next module, Neural Network Fundamentals, builds the actual, shared mechanics from the ground up, neurons, layers, weights, and forward propagation specifically, the genuine technical foundation every architecture family covered later in this course is ultimately built on top of.
10. Worked Example
The example below classifies a small dataset into the problem categories covered in this topic, illustrating how recognizing a problem's shape guides the architecture choice.

code.content:
problem_examples = [
    {"description": "Classify a photo as cat or dog", "category": "image-based"},
    {"description": "Predict tomorrow's stock price from the past 30 days", "category": "sequence-based"},
    {"description": "Generate a new image from a text description", "category": "generative"},
    {"description": "Train an agent to play a video game through repeated play", "category": "reinforcement-style"},
    {"description": "Locate every pedestrian in a street photo", "category": "image-based"},
    {"description": "Translate a sentence from English to French", "category": "sequence-based"},
]

recommended_module = {
    "image-based": "CNN and Computer Vision Tasks",
    "sequence-based": "Sequence Models, RNN, LSTM and GRU, or Transformers",
    "generative": "Generative Models",
    "reinforcement-style": "Advanced Topics (Deep Reinforcement Learning)",
}

for example in problem_examples:
    module = recommended_module[example["category"]]
    print(f"{example['description']}")
    print(f"  -> Category: {example['category']}, look toward: {module}\n")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This example is deliberately simplified into a lookup table. Real problem identification often requires more judgment, especially for the blended, multimodal problems already covered earlier in this topic.

blocks.text: 11. Introduction to Deep Learning: Module Recap

items: Image-based problems span classification, object detection, and segmentation, covered in the CNN modules ahead.
Sequence problems, where order matters, span time series and text, covered in Sequence Models, RNN, and Transformer modules.
Generative problems produce new content, covered in the Generative Models module ahead.
Reinforcement-style problems combine deep networks with trial-and-error learning, touched on in Advanced Topics.
The core skill is recognizing a problem's category first, then matching it to the right architecture family.
Every category relies on the same core mechanics: neurons, layers, activation functions, loss functions, backpropagation.
Real problems often blend categories, like image captioning, covered further in Multimodal Deep Learning.
This closes the Introduction to Deep Learning module: what it is, why it works, its history, applications, workflow, and problem types.
Next module: Neural Network Fundamentals, building the shared mechanics every architecture family in this course relies on.
